pages.text: Businesses, fire departments and the forest service use $(thing)commercial$() radios: no dial, just a $(thing)16-position channel knob$() (16 channels; the upgraded handheld holds 64, see its page). Each channel was set up by a radio shop: its receive and transmit frequencies, analog FM or digital, a CTCSS tone, and an encryption key.$(br2)You cannot change a channel on the radio itself. A radio computer's $(l:radiocraft:computer/radio_programmer)programmer$() does that, or a $(l:radiocraft:radios/radio_cloner)Radio Cloner$() copies another radio (or an operator with $(thing)/rcdebug commercial$()).

pages.title: Who is talking
pages.text: Each radio has a $(thing)unit ID$() and sends it every time it keys up: on FM as a short $(thing)brrrp$() of data at the start, on digital inside the data. The upgraded handheld and the mobiles show the caller's ID, or the name their contact list gives it ("ENG 5"), while they talk and for a few seconds after. Encrypted calls show the ID even without the key. The basic brick has no display: it only sends.

pages.title: Out of the box
pages.text: A new radio comes $(thing)blank$(), with no channels, as from a real dealer: program it with the $(l:radiocraft:computer/radio_programmer)radio programmer$(/l) before it does anything. The license-free $(thing)MURS$() channels (151.820, 151.880, 151.940, 154.570, 154.600 MHz) are a good start.$(br2)A knob position with no channel is dead: no receive, no transmit. Commercial radios always transmit inside their own band, and take no MARS mod.

pages.title: Basic Commercial Handheld
pages.text: A 1990s brick for 150-174 MHz, analog FM only. No display: TX (red), RX (green) and power (blue) lights. Sneak and use it, then scroll or drag the two knobs on top: $(thing)channel$() (1-16) and $(thing)power/volume$() (OFF switches it off). Hold right click to talk. Charges in a desk charger.

pages.title: Upgraded Commercial Handheld
pages.text: The fire-service radio: 64 channels, digital voice and encryption, and 2 m too. The same two knobs on top; the knob picks within a $(thing)zone$(), and the keys $(thing)A$() to $(thing)D$() pick the zone: A is channels 1-16, B 17-32, C 33-48, D 49-64. * shows its ID, # the frequency.

pages.title: Mobile Radios
pages.text: The $(item)Commercial VHF Mobile Radio$() (150-174 MHz, analog and digital) and the $(item)Commercial Low Band Radio$() (30-50 MHz, analog) sit on a desk, in a vehicle or on a ship, with a hand mic on a cord: sneak and use to take it. They need power and an antenna for their band, like the base stations.

pages.title: Distress beacons
pages.text: Program a VHF mobile with a channel on $(thing)161.975 MHz$() and turn the knob to it: it decodes $(l:radiocraft:radios/distress_beacon)distress beacon$(/l) alerts. A new one sounds an alarm and the display shows $(thing)DISTRESS DETECTED 161.975$() and the beacon's coordinates until you clear it: sneak and use the radio. Cabled to a computer, the $(l:radiocraft:computer/distress)DISTRESS$(/l) program lists them.

pages.title: Digital voice
pages.text: Digital has no static at all: it is perfectly clean until the signal is about as weak as FM would be with 70% static, warbles for a moment, then drops out.$(br2)An $(thing)encrypted$() channel needs the same key at the other end. Without it you hear garbled digital noise; on an analog or ham radio a digital signal is a harsh buzz. A repeater passes it on as it is.

pages.title: Paint
pages.text: The cases take dye like leather armour: craft a radio with dyes to colour it (the knobs, antenna, battery, grille and keypad stay black). Undyed, the brick is grey and the upgraded radio black. A mobile keeps its colour and its channels when you break it and place it again.
Upgrading a brick does not keep its channels: the new radio starts blank.
The low band mobile takes a 10 m crystal. A $(l:radiocraft:computer/frequency_manager)frequency list$(/l) can fill a whole fleet's channels.
